beats.text: Concept Bottleneck Models. From black-box predictions to interpretable, editable concepts.
We begin with the black box: what evidence did the model use, and can a person inspect it?
beats.head: Why make predictions interpretable?

beats.text: A neural network makes a prediction. How can a person inspect, and correct, the intermediate evidence it used?
beats.head: Can a person inspect, and {e:correct}, the evidence a network used?

beats.text: Here is a photograph of a gull, and a real model, CLIP. The name stands for Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training.
beats.head: A real {x:photograph} and a real model, CLIP

beats.text: It is asked to choose among six gull species, by comparing the image with a short description of each.
beats.head: CLIP compares the {x:photo} with one sentence per species

beats.text: Image in, an encoder, and a score for every species. It prefers American herring gull, with a softmax share of 0.54. Glaucous-winged gull comes second, at 0.21.
beats.head: The {x:photo} goes in, a {y:score} for every species comes out

beats.text: The answer happens to be right. But what made the model prefer it?
beats.head: The answer is right. What made the model prefer it?

beats.text: A common response is a heatmap. This one is computed: we grey out one patch of the photograph at a time, and measure how much the herring gull score drops.
beats.head: Occlusion: grey out one {x:patch}, measure the {y:score} drop

beats.text: The largest drops sit on the bill and the head.
beats.head: The largest drops sit on the bill and the head

beats.text: So what did the model recognise there? The yellow bill? The red spot near its tip? The shape of the head? Or the blue water just behind it?
beats.head: Which property did the model recognise there?

beats.text: The map marks where the score is sensitive. It does not say which property the model detected, and it gives a person nothing specific to correct.
beats.head: The map shows where the {y:score} is sensitive, not which property

beats.text: Suppose instead the model had to state its evidence as named properties: wingtip colour, bill shape, head colour. Each claim could then be checked.
beats.head: What we want: evidence stated as named {c:properties}

beats.text: There are two ways to get an explanation from a model. You can train a black box and explain it afterwards, which is called post-hoc. Or you can build the model so that its reasoning can be read from the start, which is called ante-hoc, or interpretable by design.
beats.head: Two routes: explain a model afterwards, or build one you can read

beats.text: Start with post-hoc. The model f is already trained. An explanation method takes the model and one input, and returns some evidence about the prediction.
beats.head: Post-hoc: a method explains a {f:trained model} on one {x:input}

beats.text: Start with a real zebra photo and a trained image classifier, a Residual Network with 50 layers, or ResNet-50. Choose its zebra score before softmax. Keep the model fixed and slightly increase the red value at the marked pixel. The zebra score changes by a tiny amount; the predicted class need not change. Sensitivity is the size of the score change divided by the size of the pixel change. In symbols, x i is one pixel channel, s k is the chosen class score, and the derivative measures sensitivity to an infinitesimal nudge. The numerical ratio shown here is an approximation.
beats.head: Saliency: nudge one {x:pixel}, watch one {y:class score}

beats.text: Keep this exact photo and model. After softmax, zebra is the top prediction; tiger has a very low probability. First choose zebra: backpropagate its score to every input pixel and show the largest absolute gradient across the colour channels. Brighter means a larger sensitivity; this gives the zebra saliency map. Now choose tiger and repeat, without changing the photo or the model. Its score is low, but it can still be sensitive to pixels. Both maps use one brightness scale and neither has been smoothed. Notice the background lights up too. A saliency map shows which tiny pixel changes affect a chosen score; it does not mean that a tiger is present, or trace the outline of the animal.
beats.head: Same {x:photo}, same model, a different {y:class to explain}

beats.text: A second family changes the input. Grey out one patch, run the model again, and measure how much the score drops. That is the occlusion map we computed for the gull in Part 1.
beats.head: Occlusion: grey out a {x:patch} and measure how far the {y:score} drops

beats.text: The input is a gull photo. A trained model produces class scores; choose the herring gull score as the output to explain. The explanation method takes the photo, the model and this choice of class. For plain gradient saliency, it computes the pixel sensitivities from the formula we just saw. It displays them as a heatmap, with brighter pixels more sensitive. This is an explanation of the score, not another prediction.
beats.head: From an {x:input photo} and a {y:class score} to a heatmap

beats.text: Now keep the photo, the herring gull class and the explanation method fixed. Compare the heatmap from the trained model with one made after replacing its learned weights with random values. For some methods, such as guided backpropagation, Adebayo and colleagues found the maps barely changed. That is a warning: the picture can survive even after learning is removed. Before trusting a heatmap, check that it depends on the learned weights. Plain gradients did change in their test, but passing this check alone does not prove an explanation is correct.
beats.head: Does the heatmap depend on what the {f:model} learned?

beats.text: Zech and colleagues studied a chest X-ray classifier. Focus on the model trained using data from both Mount Sinai and the National Institutes of Health Clinical Center, or NIH. Each training example pairs an X-ray with a pneumonia label derived from its radiology report. The label says whether pneumonia is reported. In the collected datasets, about a third of Mount Sinai X-rays have a positive label, compared with about one in a hundred at NIH. These are dataset label rates, not rates for all hospital patients. At test time, a new X-ray goes into the trained model, without its label, and a pneumonia score comes out. The intended clue is disease in the lungs, but the hospital already gives a clue to the label. That is the shortcut we will examine next.
beats.head: The setup: learn {y:pneumonia} from two {x:hospital datasets}

beats.text: A network could tell which hospital an X-ray came from almost perfectly, from markers and scanner details rather than from the lungs. Since the hospital predicts pneumonia, the detector could use the hospital as a shortcut.
beats.head: The network could tell which {k:hospital} an X-ray came from

beats.text: A heatmap might light up the hospital marker in the corner, and expose the shortcut. But it cannot remove it. On X-rays from a third hospital, the detector did worse. The only fix was new data and retraining.
beats.head: An explanation can expose the {k:shortcut}, but the fix is new data

beats.text: The third limit is vocabulary. A heatmap says where the score was sensitive. It does not say what the model saw there. On the gull: the yellow bill, the red spot, or the shape of the head?
beats.head: Limit 3: a heatmap says {x:where}, not {c:what}

beats.text: Experts reason in named findings: a narrowed joint space, a bone spur, black wingtips. Even when an expert spots the mistake, the model has no named part to correct. There is no setting for wingtip colour that a person could switch from grey to black.
beats.head: Experts speak in {c:findings}, and the model has no knob for them

beats.text: Ante-hoc models take the other route. The prediction is computed from quantities a person can read. A sparse linear model on named features is one example. A short decision tree is another. Prototype networks compare parts of an image with stored example parts.
beats.head: Ante-hoc: the prediction is computed from quantities a person can read

beats.text: Rudin argued that for high-stakes decisions we should prefer models like these over black boxes explained afterwards.
beats.head: The case for models that are interpretable by design

beats.text: A concept bottleneck model is an ante-hoc model for deep networks. First, predict named properties of the photo, its concepts. Then predict the answer from those concepts alone.
beats.head: A concept bottleneck predicts {c:concepts} first, then the {y:answer}

beats.text: In symbols: x is the input, c hat is the vector of predicted concepts, and y hat is the prediction. A concept predictor, g, maps x to c hat. A task head, f, maps c hat to y hat.
beats.head: The same path in symbols

beats.text: Now we put named concepts between the image and the prediction.
beats.head: The concept bottleneck

beats.text: Here is that idea on a real photograph, with numbers small enough to follow. Between the image and the answer, we insert a layer of named variables.
beats.head: Here is that idea on a real {x:photograph}

beats.text: A concept predictor, g theta, maps the image to a vector of concept values, c hat. A task head, f phi, maps those values to the prediction, y hat.
beats.head: A {x:concept predictor} fills the layer, a {f:task head} reads it

beats.text: Here the concepts are wingtip grey, wingtip black, bill pointed, head white, and tail rounded. Each receives a value between 0 and 1.
beats.head: The {c:concept vector} has five named entries

beats.text: The essential rule: the task head receives only these five numbers. No other path from the image reaches it. That narrow interface is the bottleneck.
beats.head: The rule: the {f:task head} reads only these five numbers

beats.text: A black box maps the image straight to an answer. A strict concept bottleneck model, or CBM, first predicts the concepts, then predicts the task from the concepts alone.
beats.head: A strict CBM predicts the {c:concepts} first, then the {y:answer} from them alone

beats.text: These concept values and this head are written by hand, for teaching.
beats.head: The {c:values} and the {f:head} on these slides are written by hand

beats.text: This model believes the wingtips are grey, at 0.8, and black, at only 0.2. So it ranks glaucous-winged gull first, 0.71 against 0.29.
beats.head: The model believes the wingtips are grey, so it says {y:glaucous-winged gull}

beats.text: Look at the photograph: the wingtips are black. An observer corrects the wing colour concepts. Grey becomes 0, and black becomes 1.
beats.head: The wingtips are black: an observer {e:corrects} the wing colour

beats.text: The task head is unchanged. It simply recomputes, and American herring gull now receives 0.91.
beats.head: The same {f:task head} recomputes, and {y:herring gull} now leads

beats.text: A person edited an intermediate belief, and the prediction followed.
beats.head: An {e:edited} belief, a new prediction

beats.text: Compare multi-task learning, where a concept head sits beside the class head.
beats.head: Multi-task learning puts a {c:concept head} beside the class head

beats.text: Editing that concept output changes nothing, because the class head never reads it.
beats.head: There, an {e:edit} to the concepts changes nothing

beats.text: In a concept bottleneck, the concepts lie on the path to the prediction.
beats.head: In a CBM, the {c:concepts} lie on the path to the {y:prediction}

beats.text: The gull is not a random choice. The standard benchmark for concept bottlenecks is a bird dataset: Caltech-UCSD Birds, or CUB.
beats.head: The standard benchmark for {c:concept bottlenecks} is a bird dataset

beats.text: It has 11,788 photographs of 200 species. Eight of the species are gulls.
beats.head: Many photographs of many similar species

beats.text: People annotated every photograph with 312 yes-or-no attributes, in 28 groups: bill shape, wing colour, wing pattern, eye colour, and so on.
beats.head: Every photograph is described by the same {c:attributes}

beats.text: Each attribute is a question with a yes or no answer. Does this bird have a hooked bill? Is its wing grey? Yes is a one, and no is a zero.
beats.head: Each attribute is a yes-or-no question

beats.text: Annotators also recorded how sure they were: definitely, probably, guessing, or not visible. About one label in ten is not visible.
beats.head: Annotators also recorded how sure they were

beats.text: Labels on single photos are noisy, so Koh and colleagues took a majority vote within each species. After the vote, every photo of a herring gull has the same labels.
beats.head: Single photos are noisy: take a vote within each {y:species}

beats.text: They then kept the 112 attributes that are present in at least ten species.
beats.head: Keep only the attributes that many species share

beats.text: One training record is a photograph, 112 zeros and ones, and a species.
beats.head: One training record has three parts

beats.text: In symbols, the concept labels c form a vector with 112 entries, each zero or one, and the label y is one of 200 species. The model predicts c hat, a value between zero and one for each concept.
beats.head: The same record in symbols

beats.text: Before building a bottleneck, we need to decide what counts as a concept.
beats.head: What is a concept?

beats.text: Let us slow down. What exactly is a concept? It is more than a neuron with a name attached: it is a promise that a person can check the claim in the input.
beats.head: A {c:concept} is a claim that a person can check

beats.text: Three things must be in place. The first is meaning: a definition that a domain expert can apply. For example, grey wingtip: the tips of the folded flight feathers are grey, not black.
beats.head: Meaning: a definition that an expert can apply

beats.text: The second is grounding: where in the input is the evidence? For wingtip colour, it is this region. The estimate should depend on these feathers, and not on the water or the rock.
beats.head: Grounding: the evidence sits in one region of the {x:photo}

beats.text: The third is representation: how the concept becomes a number. The simplest is binary: c j is zero or one.
beats.head: Representation: the simplest {c:concept} is binary

beats.text: A soft concept passes a logit, z, through the sigmoid, giving a value between zero and one. A logit of 1.4 gives 0.80.
beats.head: A soft {c:concept} turns a logit into a value between 0 and 1

beats.text: A soft score of 0.8 is not automatically a calibrated probability. Whether eighty percent of such cases really have grey wingtips has to be checked on data.
beats.head: A soft score is not automatically a probability

beats.text: Some concepts are categorical. Wing colour takes one value from a list, so its scores form a softmax over the options, and they sum to one.
beats.head: Categorical: one value from a list, with scores that sum to 1

beats.text: Others are continuous, such as bill length in millimetres, predicted by regression.
beats.head: Continuous: a measurement, such as bill length

beats.text: Richer models give each concept a vector, an embedding, or a whole probability distribution. We will meet these in Part 10.
beats.head: Richer {c:concepts}: a vector or a whole distribution

beats.text: And sometimes the evidence is missing. In CUB, a wingtip hidden behind a rock is labelled not visible. Unknown is not the same as absent, and the representation should be able to say so.
beats.head: Unknown: not visible is different from absent

beats.text: So a concept can be stored in six ways: binary, soft, categorical, continuous, a vector or distribution, and unknown.
beats.head: Six ways to store a {c:concept} as a number

beats.text: The same pattern applies across sensors. In a sleep EEG recording, a concept might be: sleep spindle present.
beats.head: The same pattern in a sleep {x:EEG} recording

beats.text: A spindle is a brief burst of brain waves, about 11 to 16 cycles per second, lasting roughly half a second to two seconds. Sleep scorers treat spindles as a sign of stage two sleep.
beats.head: A {c:spindle} is a brief burst of brain waves

beats.text: In a customer message, a concept might be: duplicate charge reported, meaning the customer says one purchase was billed twice.
beats.head: The same pattern in a customer {x:message}

beats.text: Each is a named claim about the input that a specialist could check.
beats.head: Each {c:concept} is a named claim that a specialist can check

scenes.title: Part 4: From concepts to a prediction

beats.text: Next, we follow one image from its predicted concepts to class scores and probabilities.
beats.head: From concepts to a prediction

scenes.title: From concepts to predictions: the arithmetic

beats.text: Start with an image. The concept predictor estimates the concepts in it. The task head reads those estimates and produces class scores. Softmax converts the scores into class probabilities. The task head can be a single linear layer or a multilayer perceptron, an MLP. We will use one linear layer so that we can see every calculation.
beats.head: Follow the {x:image} all the way to {y:class probabilities}

beats.text: Our possible classes are zebra, horse and giraffe. For every image, we predict the same three concepts, in this order: stripes, horse-like shape and long neck. These concept names are fixed before we train the model.
beats.head: Three {y:classes} and three {c:concepts}

beats.text: The concept predictor, g theta, is a neural network that takes the image as input. For this hand-chosen example, suppose it predicts stripes 0.1, horse-like shape 0.9 and long neck 0.1. These are assumed outputs for this photograph, not measurements from a trained network. Together they form c hat, the predicted concept vector for this image. The hat means predicted.
beats.head: The {x:concept predictor} turns this image into three {c:estimates}

beats.text: Now pass that same concept vector to the task head, f phi. It takes the three concept values and returns one score for each class. Its input is the predicted concepts. It does not see the image directly. This is where we could use a linear layer or an MLP.
beats.head: The {f:task head} turns predicted {c:concepts} into {y:class scores}

beats.text: For our example, choose a single linear layer with no bias. Its weight table, W, has a row for each class and a column for each concept. The zebra row is 3, 1, 0. These are weights, not another image's concept values. We normally learn the weights during training and keep them fixed when predicting new images. Here, both the weights and the concept values are hand-chosen to make the arithmetic easy.
beats.head: The {c:concept values} describe this image; the {f:weights} belong to the layer

beats.text: Let us compute just the zebra score. Stripes contributes 3 times 0.1, which is 0.3. Horse-like shape contributes 1 times 0.9, which is 0.9. Long neck contributes 0 times 0.1, which is 0. Add these contributions to get 1.2. This is one output of the linear layer.
beats.head: Inside the layer: multiply each {c:concept value} by its {f:weight}, then add

beats.text: Repeat that calculation with the horse row and the giraffe row. The layer returns zebra 1.2, horse 1.6 and giraffe 0.2. These scores are also called logits. Only now do we write the shorthand: scores equal W times c hat. This is just the linear layer applied to the predicted concept vector.
beats.head: The same layer produces all three {y:class scores}

beats.text: Pass the score vector through softmax. Exponentiate each score and divide by the total. This gives class probabilities that sum to one. Horse has the largest score, 1.6, and the largest probability, about 0.52. The predicted class is horse.
beats.head: Softmax turns the {y:scores} into {y:class probabilities}

beats.text: Now an observer looks at the image and sees stripes. They correct the stripes value from 0.1 to 1. The other concept values stay the same. This edit replaces one entry in the predicted concept vector.
beats.head: A person {e:corrects} one predicted {c:concept}

beats.text: Feed the corrected concept vector into the same linear layer. Its weights have not changed. The new scores are zebra 3.9, horse 0.7 and giraffe minus 0.7. The image and the concept predictor are unchanged. We only replace one concept value before running the task head again.
beats.head: Pass the {e:corrected concepts} through the same {f:layer}

beats.text: Apply softmax to the new scores. Zebra now has probability about 0.95. The predicted class changes from horse to zebra.
beats.head: After softmax, {y:zebra} has the highest probability

beats.text: Only the stripes value changed, by 0.9. The zebra weight for stripes is 3. So the zebra score increases by 3 times 0.9, which is 2.7. That takes it from 1.2 to 3.9. The other contributions stay the same.
beats.head: Why did the {y:zebra score} rise?

beats.text: The full path is still image, concept predictor, concept vector, task head, scores and softmax. A person can correct a concept in the middle, then run the same task head again. The answer can change without retraining either network.
beats.head: The {c:concept vector} is the point where a person can {e:intervene}

beats.text: We now compare how the concept predictor and task head learn from their labels.
beats.head: Learning the concepts

scenes.title: How does the model learn the concepts?

beats.text: So far the concept values were given. Where do they come from? The concept predictor learns them from labelled examples.
beats.head: Where do the {c:concept values} come from?

beats.text: Each training example carries three things: an input x i, concept labels c i, and a task label y i. For a herring gull in CUB: the photo, zeros and ones, and the species.
beats.head: Each training example carries three things

beats.text: The concept loss, L c, compares the predicted concepts with the labels: typically a binary cross-entropy for each concept, averaged.
beats.head: The {l:concept loss} compares each {c:predicted concept} with its {c:label}

beats.text: One term: grey wing has label 1; suppose the predictor says 0.8. The term is minus log 0.8, about 0.22. Closer to 1 costs less.
beats.head: One {l:term} of the {l:concept loss}, worked out

beats.text: The task loss, L y, is typically a cross-entropy over the classes: minus the log of the share given to the correct class.
beats.head: The {l:task loss} compares the prediction with the {y:task label}

beats.text: A weighted sum combines the two; lambda c and lambda y set how much each counts.
beats.head: A weighted sum combines the two {l:losses}

beats.text: In the original paper, Koh and colleagues compared three ways to train.
beats.head: Three ways to train the {x:concept predictor} and the {f:task head}

beats.text: Independent: fit the predictor to the concept labels, and separately fit the head on the true concepts. At test time, though, the head receives predicted concepts.
beats.head: Independent: each part is trained on its own labels

beats.text: Sequential: fit the predictor, freeze it, then fit the head on the concepts it predicts. The head learns from the predictor's actual mistakes.
beats.head: Sequential: freeze the {x:predictor}, then train the {f:head} on its outputs

beats.text: Joint: train the whole system at once, with both losses.
beats.head: Joint: train the whole system at once, with both {l:losses}

beats.text: In joint training, the task loss sends its gradient back through the head and the concept values into the predictor, which is then shaped by what helps the task.
beats.head: In joint training, the {l:task loss} also shapes the {x:concept predictor}

beats.text: That can improve task accuracy. It can also hurt concept fidelity, if a concept score drifts toward whatever helps the classifier. That has to be measured.
beats.head: A {c:concept score} can be pulled two ways

beats.text: The experiment we will meet later used joint training, with the concept loss weighted 2 and the task loss weighted 1.
beats.head: Our measured run: joint training, $\lambda_c = 2$, $\lambda_y = 1$

beats.text: Part 5 described three training schemes. Does the choice matter on real photographs? We ran a small version on CUB.
beats.head: Does the training scheme matter on real photographs?

beats.text: Each photo goes through a frozen CLIP image encoder, giving 512 features. A linear concept predictor maps them to 112 concepts, and a linear task head maps those to 200 species.
beats.head: Our setup: {x:frozen CLIP features} → {c:112 concepts} → {y:200 species}

beats.text: For our gull photo, the predictor is sure the throat is white and the wings are grey. The head spreads its probability over several gull species.
beats.head: One photo through the model: {x:features}, then {c:concepts}, then {y:species}

beats.text: Joint training is the most accurate, close to a standard model with no bottleneck. Sequential falls in between, and independent training is the least accurate.
beats.head: Joint training is the most accurate, independent the least

beats.text: Now intervene. Pick a few attribute groups, replace their predicted values with the true values, and let the same head recompute.
beats.head: An intervention replaces {c:predicted values} with {e:true values}

beats.text: The independent model improves fastest. Its head was trained on true concepts, so it trusts corrected ones. The joint model improves least.
beats.head: As more groups are {e:corrected}, the independent model gains most

beats.text: Next, a person corrects a concept and we follow the effect on the prediction.
beats.head: Human interventions

beats.text: Concepts are useful because a person can check them. When the model gets one wrong, someone who can see the mistake can correct it, with no retraining.
beats.head: A person can fix a {c:concept} the model got wrong

beats.text: An intervention has four steps. The model predicts concept values. A person checks one and corrects it. The fixed task head recomputes. A new prediction comes out.
beats.head: An intervention has four steps

beats.text: Back to the gull. Wing colour is a categorical concept, so the observer corrects the group together: grey to 0, black to 1.
beats.head: Wing colour is one group: {e:correct it together}

beats.text: Changing only one of them could leave an impossible state, with both colours on, or neither.
beats.head: Changing only one value could leave an impossible state

beats.text: The head's score for American herring gull moves from 0.29 to 0.91.
beats.head: Same {f:head}, new {c:values}: herring gull rises

beats.text: The same mechanism works on a signal. Here is a schematic EEG trace, drawn for teaching rather than recorded from a patient. Near the middle is a short burst at about 13 hertz, the shape of a sleep spindle.
beats.head: The same mechanism works on a {x:signal}

beats.text: The concept predictor gives spindle present only 0.12. K-complex present gets 0.8, and slow-wave dominance 0.15.
beats.head: The {x:concept predictor} gives {c:spindle} a low value

beats.text: With these values, an illustrative stage head favours other stage, at 0.62, over an N2 candidate, at 0.38.
beats.head: An illustrative {f:stage head} favours other stage

beats.text: A sleep expert inspects the trace and marks the spindle as present. 0.12 becomes 1.
beats.head: A sleep expert {e:marks the spindle as present}

beats.text: Same head, new input. The N2 candidate rises to 0.86.
beats.head: Same {f:head}, new input: {y:N2 candidate} rises

beats.text: This demonstrates the mechanism, not a clinical result. Real sleep staging applies scoring rules to thirty-second epochs, and this head was written by hand.
beats.head: A demonstration of the mechanism, not a clinical result

scenes.title: Part 7: When a correct edit hurts

beats.text: A correct concept edit can still hurt the final prediction, so we need to understand how the head uses it.
beats.head: When a correct edit hurts

scenes.title: A correct edit can still hurt

beats.text: So far, every correction has helped. Does a correct edit always help? Here is a case where it does not.
beats.head: Does a correct edit always help?

beats.text: A support message reads: The app works, but I was charged twice. Please refund the extra payment. It belongs in the billing queue.
beats.head: A support message that belongs in {y:billing}

beats.text: The concept predictor rates duplicate charge at only 0.2, and refund requested at 1.
beats.head: The {x:concept predictor} reads two {c:concepts} from the message

beats.text: The task head computes a billing score. It starts at 1.2, takes away 2 for each unit of duplicate charge, and adds 0.6 for each unit of refund requested.
beats.head: The {f:task head}, in words

beats.text: In symbols, the score s is 1.2, minus 2 times duplicate charge, plus 0.6 times refund requested. A sigmoid turns that score into the billing share.
beats.head: The same {f:head} in symbols

beats.text: Before any edit, the score is 1.2, minus 0.4, plus 0.6, which gives 1.4. Billing receives 0.80, so the message is already routed correctly.
beats.head: Before the edit, the message goes to {y:billing}

beats.text: A reviewer reads the message and correctly sets duplicate charge to 1.
beats.head: A reviewer {e:correctly} sets duplicate charge to 1

beats.text: Now the score is 1.2, minus 2, plus 0.6, which gives minus 0.2. Billing falls to 0.45, and the message goes to general support.
beats.head: After the edit, the message leaves {y:billing}

beats.text: The edit was correct. The fault lies downstream: this head learned a negative weight for duplicate charge, the wrong sign for billing.
beats.head: The fault is in the {f:head}: a weight with the wrong sign

beats.text: Correcting a concept does not repair an incorrect decision rule. An intervention is only as good as the head that receives it, so its effect has to be measured rather than assumed.
beats.head: Correcting a {c:concept} does not repair the {f:decision rule}

beats.text: This head was built faulty on purpose, to show that the failure can happen. It says nothing about how often it does.
beats.head: A constructed case: the failure can happen
