beats.head: An incomplete concept vocabulary

scenes.title: What if the concepts are incomplete?

beats.text: A second limit sits in the vocabulary itself: the bottleneck passes on only what we chose to name.
beats.head: The bottleneck can pass on only what the vocabulary names

beats.text: Take two objects, a blue circle and a blue square. They belong to different classes.
beats.head: Two objects from two different {y:classes}

beats.text: Suppose the concept vocabulary has only two entries: colour and size. Both objects are blue. Both are small.
beats.head: The vocabulary names only {c:colour} and {c:size}

beats.text: So both map to exactly the same concept vector. c of x 1 equals c of x 2, and yet y 1 differs from y 2.
beats.head: Both objects get the same {c:concept vector}

beats.text: Watch what reaches the task head. Shape was present in the image. At the bottleneck, it disappears.
beats.head: Shape never reaches the {f:task head}

beats.text: Any task head that reads only this vector must give both objects the same output. No head, linear or a large neural network, can recover a distinction that never reached it.
beats.head: The same input to the {f:head} gives the same {y:output}

beats.text: On these two examples, the best possible accuracy is fifty percent.
beats.head: The best possible accuracy is one half

beats.text: The ideal property is called sufficiency. Once the concepts are known, the input says nothing more about the label.
beats.head: Sufficiency: the {c:concepts} say all the {x:input} says about the {y:label}

beats.text: In symbols: Y is independent of X, given C. Here it fails: the label depends on shape, which C lacks.
beats.head: Sufficiency in symbols

beats.text: A strict CBM guarantees something weaker. Its own prediction depends on the input only through the concepts. Whether the true label does is a property of the chosen vocabulary.
beats.head: A strict CBM guarantees something weaker

beats.text: More accurate colour and size estimates would not help. The fix is a richer vocabulary: add shape. Now the two vectors differ.
beats.head: The fix is a richer vocabulary: add {c:shape}

beats.text: We now compare newer architectures by the supervision they need, from concept labels to class labels to no fitting on the new task.
beats.head: Modern concept bottleneck architectures

beats.text: The original concept bottleneck needs a person to label every concept on every training image. That is its main cost, and most newer methods try to reduce it.
beats.head: Labelling every {c:concept} on every {x:image} is the main cost

beats.text: One supervised training record looks like this: the image, a 0 or 1 for each named concept, and the class. On CUB, that meant 112 concept labels per photograph.
beats.head: One training record: an {x:image}, its {c:concept labels} and a {y:class}

beats.text: The newer methods form a ladder of shrinking supervision. On the first rung, CBMs and concept embedding models need the image, the concept labels and the class.
beats.head: Rung one: {x:images}, {c:concept labels} and {y:classes}

beats.text: Post-hoc models, label-free models, Language in a Bottle, or LaBo, and vision-language-guided concept bottleneck models, or VLG-CBMs, drop the concept labels on the task images. They still learn from images with class labels. A pretrained model supplies visual knowledge, and concept names can come from people or a language model.
beats.head: Rung two: keep {y:class labels}, drop per-image {c:concept labels}

beats.text: Classification by description drops training on the new task. It still uses a pretrained model. We supply class descriptions and a new image, without fitting a model to labelled examples of these classes.
beats.head: Rung three: no training for this task

beats.text: Take Language in a Bottle, or LaBo, as an example of rung two. A language model supplies descriptions, such as black and white stripes. Pretrained CLIP compares each image with these descriptions and produces match scores. During training, class labels teach a task head how to combine those scores. For a new photo, the learned head predicts the class. We need class-labelled images, but no person has to label every concept in every image. The diagram illustrates the path, without showing measured scores.
beats.head: Rung two: {y:class labels} teach the {f:task head}

beats.text: Now keep the pretrained CLIP model, but replace the learned head with a fixed rule. A language model supplies descriptions for each class. CLIP compares a new photo with each description. We average the match scores within each class and choose the class with the highest average. No class-labelled examples or fitting are needed for this task. The difference is the combination: rung two learns it from class labels; rung three uses a fixed average.
beats.head: Rung three: combine the {c:match scores} with a fixed rule

beats.text: Dropping per-image concept labels saves labelling, but removes a direct check. A person who supplies a concept label has checked it against the image. On the higher rungs, a match score alone does not establish that the named concept is visible. We need to check this another way.
beats.head: Fewer {c:concept labels}, so check the {c:concepts} another way

beats.text: So for each variant, watch for one question: who checks that a named concept is really visible in the image? We come back to it when we discuss grounding.
beats.head: For each variant, ask: is the {c:concept} really in the {x:image}?

beats.text: Newer variants change four things: where the concepts come from, how each concept is detected, how it is represented, and what reaches the task head.
beats.head: A variant can change four things

beats.text: We will walk through them on one running example: photographs of zebras, horses and giraffes, the classes from Part 4. We train on 24 photos and test on 12.
beats.head: One running example: {x:photographs} of zebras, horses and giraffes

beats.text: For each variant, we first say in one line what changed compared with the plain CBM. Then we write down how the path changes: from x, the image, to c hat, the concepts, to y hat, the class.
beats.head: For each variant: how the path from {x:image} to {c:concepts} to {y:class} changes

scenes.title: Part 10 · Rung One: Concept labels and class labels

beats.text: On rung one, every training image has concept labels and a class label; concept embedding models keep this supervision but give each concept a richer representation.
beats.head: Concept labels and class labels

beats.text: First, concept embedding models, or CEMs. One number per concept is a narrow channel, and when the vocabulary is incomplete, accuracy suffers, as we saw in Part 8.
beats.head: One number per {c:concept} is a narrow channel

beats.text: A prototype usually means a representative example. Here the clearer term is embedding: a short list of learned numbers. CEM computes a present vector and an absent vector for the current image. Both exist even when stripes are clearly visible. They are not stored example photos or fixed class averages. The coordinates are learned features, not individually labelled properties. These numbers are illustrative.
beats.head: What does a prototype mean here?

beats.text: Where do the vectors come from? An image encoder first extracts features. For stripes, two learned layers turn those features into the present and absent vectors. Every concept has its own pair of layers. Training learns the weights of these layers. With those weights fixed, a different image can still produce different vectors. Nobody supplies target values for the vector coordinates.
beats.head: Learned layers turn the {x:image} into the two {c:vectors}

beats.text: Now the mechanics. An embedding is a short list of numbers that describes something; here each one has two numbers. From the image, the model computes two embeddings for every concept: one describing it as active, one as inactive.
beats.head: Each {c:concept} gets two embeddings: active and inactive

beats.text: A learned scoring layer reads both vectors and predicts the probability, p, that the concept is present. Suppose that, as in Part 4, it misses the stripes on this photo: p is only 0.1. The concept labels will teach this probability during training.
beats.head: A learned scorer predicts the probability {c:p}

beats.text: The concept's embedding mixes the two: p times the active embedding, plus one minus p times the inactive one.
beats.head: The {c:concept embedding} mixes the two, weighted by {c:p}

beats.text: With p equal to 0.1, take the first entry: 0.1 times 0.82, plus 0.9 times 0.22, gives 0.28. The second entry works the same way, and the mixed vector sits close to inactive.
beats.head: With {c:p = 0.1}, the mixed vector sits close to inactive

beats.text: At test time, only the new image is needed. The trained model computes both vectors and a probability for every concept, then mixes them. The head reads all three mixed vectors, six numbers in all. Our illustrative linear head produces class scores, and softmax gives the displayed probabilities. Here it favours horse. All weights stay fixed, and no true concept or class label is used for this ordinary prediction.
beats.head: At test time, the {f:head} reads the mixed vectors

beats.text: To intervene, a person sets p, not the vector coordinates. Setting p to 1 swaps in the active embedding already computed for this image. The same head now makes zebra lead in this example. The two candidate vectors and all network weights stay fixed; there is no retraining.
beats.head: An optional {e:correction} changes {e:p}, with weights fixed

beats.text: During training, each image comes with concept labels and a class label. For this zebra, stripes is labelled present and the class is zebra. A concept loss compares the predicted probability with the concept label. A task loss compares the class prediction with the class label. Backpropagation from these losses updates the encoder, the vector-generating layers, the probability scorer and the task head together. We supervise the probability and the final answer, rather than supplying the vector coordinates.
beats.head: Training uses {c:concept labels} and {y:class labels}

beats.text: Compare the two stages. The input during training is an image with concept and class labels. At test time it is just a new image. The weights are updated during training and kept fixed at test time. The vectors and probabilities are computed from each image in both cases.
beats.head: Training learns the weights. Testing uses them

beats.text: In symbols, for concept j out of k: g now outputs a probability and two embeddings, each m numbers long. c hat j is the mixed vector, and f reads all of them. Training still needs images, concept labels and class labels.
beats.head: Concept embedding models in symbols

scenes.title: Part 10 · Rung Two: Class labels for the task

beats.text: We now move to rung two: the task images still need class labels, but no concept label for every image; post-hoc models build a concept bank from a separate source, such as labelled concept examples or text descriptions.
beats.head: Class labels for the task

beats.text: Second, post-hoc concept bottleneck models, or PCBMs. Instead of training a concept predictor from scratch, they reuse a pretrained encoder that already exists, so nobody has to label every concept on the task training images. We still need a source for the concept bank, which we will build next.
beats.head: Reuse a {x:pretrained encoder}; build a {c:concept bank}

beats.text: First, the intuition. A pretrained encoder already arranges photos in its feature space, and some directions in that space follow visual properties, such as how striped an animal is.
beats.head: Intuition: the {x:encoder} already arranges photos along directions

beats.text: A concept bank gives names to some of those directions. A concept score then asks one question: how far along the stripes direction is this photo?
beats.head: A {c:concept bank} names directions; a score asks how far along

beats.text: Now the details. Here the frozen encoder is CLIP's image encoder: each photograph becomes 512 numbers, which we call e of x.
beats.head: A frozen {x:image encoder} turns each photo into 512 numbers

beats.text: First choose a concept, such as stripes. Collect some images with stripes and some without stripes. These are concept examples: the labels say striped or not striped, rather than zebra or horse. They can come from a separate dataset. Pass both groups through the same frozen image encoder. Only the small concept classifier will be fitted here.
beats.head: Start with examples of one {c:concept}: stripes

beats.text: Let us replace 512 numbers with two, so each image becomes a point on a page. The axes are unnamed encoder features, not concepts. In this constructed example, striped images happen to sit on the right and unstriped images on the left. The colours show labels supplied by people. We have not trained or moved the encoder.
beats.head: For intuition, give each image just {x:two features}

beats.text: Fit a linear classifier to separate the two groups. In two dimensions its boundary is a line. Across that line, towards the striped examples, lies the direction we want. This perpendicular arrow is the concept activation vector, or CAV. It tells us which way increases the striped score. Keep this direction fixed when scoring other images.
beats.head: Fit a boundary, then name the direction across it: {c:CAV}

beats.text: Now take a new image. In our toy space its features are 1.5 and 2. The teal unit CAV arrow points one step to the right and none upwards: its entries are 1, 0. Only the horizontal coordinate contributes: 1.5 times 1 plus 2 times 0 gives 1.5. A second image at minus 0.5, 2 scores minus 0.5. A higher score means further towards the striped side. These are concept scores, not probabilities or animal classes.
beats.head: Score a new image along the {c:striped direction}

beats.text: The CAV example is complete: we fitted a concept direction from labelled image features and used it to score a new image. We now change only how we obtain that direction. Instead of fitting a classifier, send the phrase black and white stripes through CLIP's frozen text encoder. Its phrase vector is a concept direction in the same space as CLIP image features. These are separate routes for building the concept bank, not consecutive steps. Our animal example follows the phrase route from here, with both CLIP encoders frozen. With either route, we score images along the saved directions and train the task head on those scores.
beats.head: Two ways to obtain a {c:concept direction}

beats.text: How far along a direction does a photo lie? Multiply the features and the direction entry by entry, then add up the products: this is the dot product. With just two entries, it is the first entry times the first, plus the second times the second.
beats.head: A projection: multiply matching entries, then add

beats.text: Back to the real animal example. Encode each phrase once and save its vector in the concept bank. For a photo, the image encoder produces 512 features. Multiply these features by the matching entries of a phrase vector, then add, just as in our two-dimensional calculation. Repeat for all eight phrases to get eight concept scores. Both vectors have length one, so this dot product is cosine similarity. For our zebra, the raw stripes score is 0.274. These scores are not probabilities.
beats.head: Back to {x:512 features}: one score for each {c:phrase}

beats.text: Keep the prompts fixed and change only the image. Here are three held-out photos: a zebra, a horse and a giraffe. Each column uses exactly the same phrase for every photo. Each cell is the raw cosine similarity between that photo and that phrase. This gives one score per image and concept. These scores are not probabilities.
beats.head: Use the same {c:concept prompts} for every {x:image}

beats.text: Each prompt has its own usual score and its own spread. To find them, score all 24 training photos with the same prompts. Compute the average and standard deviation separately down each column, across images. Save those training statistics and reuse them for every new photo. The three test photos on the previous slide do not set the scale.
beats.head: Each {c:prompt} gets its own training average and spread

beats.text: Each cell is standardised separately. Take the zebra and stripes cell. Subtract its average over the 24 training photos, then divide by its spread, the standard deviation. For stripes, that gives 1.41.
beats.head: Standardise each score: subtract the mean, divide by the spread

beats.text: Now apply the same rule to every cell, using its column's saved mean and spread. The photos and prompts have not changed; only the units have changed. The zebra's stripes score becomes 1.41, while the giraffe's long-neck score becomes 1.70. A positive value means above that prompt's training average, zero means at the average, and a negative value means below it. A negative score does not prove that the concept is absent. Within each column, the order of the images stays the same. The head receives these standardised values.
beats.head: The same {x:photos} and {c:prompts}, now on a common scale

beats.text: These eight numbers are the concept bottleneck. Each belongs to a named phrase. For this zebra photo, black and white stripes scores highest, 1.4 standard deviations above its average on the training photos.
beats.head: For this zebra, {c:stripes} scores highest

beats.text: Now use the task training photos, each with its animal class label. The frozen encoder and concept bank turn each photo into eight scores, using the saved training scale. Feed those scores to a linear head. Compare its prediction with the true class and update only the head weights and constants. The encoder, concept directions and scaling stay fixed. This learns which named concepts help distinguish zebra, horse and giraffe.
beats.head: Train the {f:task head} using concept scores and {y:class labels}

beats.text: The head is also sparse. An L1 penalty adds the size of every weight to the loss, so weights that do not help are pushed to exactly zero. Of 24 possible weights, 8 concepts times 3 classes, only 4 are non-zero: zebra reads stripes, giraffe reads a long neck, and horse reads a flowing mane.
beats.head: Sparse: only 4 of 24 {f:weights} are non-zero

beats.text: For this zebra, only the stripes weight feeds the zebra score: the stripes score times its weight, plus the constant, gives about 2.03. The softmax turns the three scores into shares, and zebra gets 0.77.
beats.head: The {y:zebra} score: stripes score times weight, plus a constant

beats.text: At test time, give the system a new image. The frozen image encoder produces its features. The saved phrase vectors turn them into raw concept scores, and the saved training statistics put the scores on the same scale. The trained head produces class scores; softmax gives probabilities. No concept labels or class label are supplied, and nothing is fitted again. This is the complete prediction path.
beats.head: At test time: one new image, with all weights fixed

beats.text: All 12 held-out photos are classified correctly. This is a tiny teaching example, not a benchmark.
beats.head: All 12 held-out photos are classified correctly

beats.text: Lower the stripes score to its usual value on other animals, and zebra falls to 0.14.
beats.head: {e:Edit} the stripes score, and zebra falls

beats.text: The concept list may miss useful evidence in the image. The hybrid post-hoc concept bottleneck model, or PCBM-h, adds a residual: an extra linear head that reads the same image features directly. Add its class scores to the concept head's scores, then apply softmax. For our zebra, the score is about 2.03 plus 0.31, giving 2.34 before softmax. During training, keep the concept model fixed and fit only the extra head using class labels. At test time, both paths read the same image. This can improve prediction when the concept list is incomplete.
beats.head: PCBM-h adds an {k:extra path} for evidence the concepts miss

beats.text: Now lower the stripes score, just as before. The concept head sees the edit, but the residual still reads the same image features, so its contribution stays unchanged. After the same edit, the concept model gives zebra probability 0.14; with the residual it is 0.20. The prediction can still change, but some evidence bypasses the concepts. The trade-off is better predictive capacity with less control through named concepts.
beats.head: An {e:edit} leaves the {k:extra path} unchanged

beats.text: Compared with the plain CBM, three of the four things changed. The concepts come from a bank of phrases instead of people, a frozen encoder and a projection replace the trained predictor, and in the hybrid a residual also reaches the head. Each concept is still one number.
beats.head: Compared with the plain CBM: the {c:concepts} come from phrases

beats.text: In symbols, for concept j out of k: g is a frozen encoder followed by a projection onto the direction v j. f is sparse and linear, plus a residual, r, in the hybrid. Only f is trained, from images and class labels.
beats.head: Post-hoc concept bottleneck models in symbols

beats.text: The third variant is the label-free concept bottleneck model, or LF-CBM. A supervised bottleneck needs a person to label every concept on every photo, 112 of them for each bird in CUB. Label-free models need no human concept labels.
beats.head: Concept labels are expensive: can a bottleneck do without them?

beats.text: Here is the intuition. CLIP is the teacher: it has learned from images paired with captions, so it can score how well any phrase matches any image. The student is a frozen ResNet with one linear layer on top, and it learns to copy the teacher's scores. A language model writes the exam questions: the phrases to score.
beats.head: The intuition: a {x:student} learns to copy a {x:teacher}'s scores

beats.text: The method has five steps. The language model proposes phrases, CLIP filters and scores them, the student learns to copy the scores, and a sparse final layer, trained with the class labels, turns them into a class.
beats.head: Five steps, from phrases to a sparse {f:final layer}

beats.text: Step one: ask a language model, for each class, for its most important features, the things commonly seen around it, and its superclasses, the broader groups it belongs to. Here is the real reply for zebra to the first question, as JSON.
beats.head: Step 1: ask a language model about each {y:class}

beats.text: Three questions for each of three classes give 59 candidate concepts.
beats.head: Three questions for three classes give 59 candidate {c:concepts}

beats.text: Step two: filter. Phrases that contain a class name go, such as zebras or horse-like body. Equine goes as a near-duplicate of equine animal. Leather saddle and ossicones on head go because even the photos that match them best score low with CLIP. 34 concepts remain.
beats.head: Step 2: drop class names, duplicates and phrases CLIP barely sees

beats.text: Step three: CLIP scores every image against every remaining concept. A higher score means the phrase fits the image better. On training images, these scores are the teacher's answers: targets for the student, not labels from a person. Follow the highlighted zebra row into step four, starting with 0.274 for stripes. This is our held-out example photo.
beats.head: Step 3: the {x:teacher}, CLIP, scores every image against every {c:concept}

beats.text: Keep the highlighted zebra row from step three. These five numbers are still CLIP's raw scores, in exactly the same concept order. The student reads the same photo through a frozen residual network, ResNet-50. Its 2048 features pass through a learned linear projection, with weights W c, to produce 34 concept activations. Training changes only the projection, so each activation follows its teacher score across training images. This held-out zebra illustrates the connection; it is not used to fit the model. The student's outputs need not equal the raw CLIP numbers. Next, put the two outputs on a comparable scale.
beats.head: Step 4: keep the {x:teacher row}, build the {c:student}

beats.text: Take the first entry of the same zebra row: CLIP's stripes score, 0.274. To standardise it, subtract the training-photo average and divide by the spread, the standard deviation. That gives 1.41. Standardise the student's stripes activation using its own training-photo average and spread: it gives 1.36. The values need not be identical; learning aims to match how this concept rises and falls across photos.
beats.head: Follow the {c:stripes} entry onto a comparable scale

beats.text: What does copying mean? Take one concept, black and white stripes. Across many images, the student's activation should be high where CLIP's score is high, and low where it is low. Only this pattern across images matters, not the exact values.
beats.head: Copying means each {c:activation} rises and falls with its {x:CLIP score}

beats.text: Before the comparison, every standardised value is cubed: multiplied by itself three times. Cubing stretches the extremes: a score two standard deviations above average becomes eight, while half a standard deviation shrinks to one eighth. So the images that CLIP scores highest count the most.
beats.head: Cubing stretches the images where {x:CLIP} scores highest

beats.text: To compare two lists of numbers, we use the cosine: multiply them entry by entry, add up, and divide by the two lengths. It is 1 when the lists rise and fall together, even if one is twice the other, near 0 when they are unrelated, and negative when they move in opposite directions.
beats.head: A cosine asks whether two lists rise and fall together

beats.text: Now the match for concept j, such as stripes. Let q bar be the student's standardised activations across the images, and P bar for CLIP's standardised scores. The match is the cosine between their cubes. W c is trained to make this match large for every concept. It needs no labels, so every unlabelled photo can help.
beats.head: The match for one {c:concept}: a cosine between cubed scores

beats.text: Step five: a final layer from concepts to classes, trained with the class labels. An L1 penalty on the weights pushes most of them to exactly zero, which is what sparse means. 6 of 102 weights survive. Zebra reads black and white stripes, and giraffe reads extremely long neck. Horse reads muscular equine build and riding bridle, and safari vehicles counts against it.
beats.head: Step 5: a sparse {f:final layer} keeps 6 of 102 weights

beats.text: Here is one prediction. For this zebra, the zebra score is 1.46 times the stripes activation, 1.36, plus a little from wildebeest herds and a small constant: 2.02 in all. Horse gets minus 0.4 and giraffe about 0. As shares, zebra gets 0.82.
beats.head: One prediction: the {f:weights} turn {c:activations} into a {y:class} score

beats.text: Why insist on sparsity? A dense layer would use all 102 weights, and nobody can check 102 numbers behind every decision. Six weights can be read in a few seconds, and each one is a claim a person can check, such as: black and white stripes count for zebra.
beats.head: Why sparse: a person can read 6 {f:weights}, not 102

beats.text: Reading them also shows a risk. Riding bridle, safari vehicles and wildebeest herds describe the setting, not the animal, so the head uses context as evidence. A horse photographed beside a safari vehicle would lose evidence for horse.
beats.head: Reading the weights shows a risk: three {c:concepts} describe the setting

beats.text: Compared with the plain concept bottleneck, a language model names the concepts instead of a person, and the concept layer learns to copy CLIP instead of learning from concept labels. The head is still trained with class labels. So label-free does not mean unsupervised: the language model, CLIP and the class labels all supervise it.
beats.head: What changed compared with the plain CBM

beats.text: In symbols: g is the frozen backbone e followed by the learned linear layer W c, fitted to CLIP's scores with the cosine of cubes. f is a sparse linear layer. The data: images and class labels, no concept labels.
beats.head: LF-CBM in symbols

beats.text: Label-free models train a linear layer to imitate CLIP. Fourth, LaBo, short for Language in a Bottle, asks a language model for concepts too, but keeps CLIP itself as the concept detector.
beats.head: LaBo keeps {x:CLIP} itself as the {c:concept} detector

beats.text: The intuition is simple. Describe each class in a few short sentences, let CLIP read them, and use its similarity scores directly as the concepts, written as 100 times CLIP's cosine. For our zebra photo, the stripes sentence scores higher than the mane sentence and the neck sentence.
beats.head: The intuition: let {x:CLIP} read short {c:sentences} about each {y:class}

beats.text: The method has four steps. A language model writes sentences, a selection rule keeps the most useful ones, CLIP scores each image against them, and a linear head, started from a guess, turns the scores into a class.
beats.head: Four steps, from sentences to a {f:head} that starts from a guess

beats.text: In step one, the language model writes eight short sentences for each class, as JSON. Here they are for zebra.
beats.head: Step 1: a language model describes each {y:class} in sentences

beats.text: Which sentences should we keep? First, each one should separate its class from the others. Take a sentence's average CLIP score on the zebra training photos, and subtract its average on the best other class. Bold black and white stripes has the widest margin of the eight. Stocky horse-like body matches another class better than zebras, so it separates nothing.
beats.head: A good set of {c:sentences} separates the classes

beats.text: Second, the set should not say the same thing three times. Once one stripes sentence is in, a second stripes sentence adds much less that is new.
beats.head: A good set of {c:sentences} does not repeat itself

beats.text: Step two puts numbers on both ideas. Discriminability is the margin from two slides back, rescaled within the class so that the best sentence gets 1 and the worst gets 0. Large striped ears lands at 0.66.
beats.head: Step 2: score each {c:sentence}'s discriminability

beats.text: Coverage gain measures what a sentence adds beyond the sentences already chosen. A greedy rule builds the set one sentence at a time: each round it takes the best mix, 0.7 times discriminability plus 0.3 times coverage gain, and keeps that choice.
beats.head: A greedy rule balances discriminability and coverage

beats.text: In round one, bold black and white stripes scores 0.7 times 1, plus 0.3 times 0.69, which is 0.91, the best of the eight. Unique facial stripe patterns comes second, then large striped ears.
beats.head: The greedy picks for zebra, in order

beats.text: For horse, a long flowing mane leads. For giraffe, an extremely long vertical neck.
beats.head: Three {c:sentences} per class, nine in all

beats.text: Step three: CLIP scores the image against the nine chosen sentences. Those nine numbers are the bottleneck. Score j compares CLIP's encoding of the image, phi of x, with its encoding of sentence j, psi of s j.
beats.head: Step 3: {x:CLIP} scores the image against each chosen {c:sentence}

beats.text: Step four: a linear layer from sentences to classes, started from a language prior, a starting guess taken from the sentences. Each class gives one third to each of its own three sentences, and nothing to the others.
beats.head: Step 4: a language prior links each {y:class} to its {c:sentences}

beats.text: So each class score is the average of its own three sentence scores. For this zebra, zebra gets 28.1, horse 22.9 and giraffe 23.7. As shares, zebra gets 0.98, and 11 of the 12 test photos are right.
beats.head: With the prior, a {y:class} score is the average of its own {c:sentence} scores

beats.text: Why start from a prior? A head that starts from zero must learn from the labels which sentence belongs to which class, and that is hard with few labelled photos. The prior already encodes it. A linear probe is a linear layer on CLIP's image features, with no concepts. The LaBo paper reports its clearest advantage over a linear probe with one labelled photo per class.
beats.head: Why a prior helps when labels are few

beats.text: After that, training with the class labels moves the weights a little, and then all 12 are right.
beats.head: Training with the {y:class labels} adjusts the weights

beats.text: Notice the zebra sentences: all three are about stripes. Is CLIP detecting striped ears, or stripes anywhere in the picture? The scores alone cannot tell.
beats.head: Do the zebra {c:sentences} detect the ears, or stripes anywhere?

beats.text: Compared with the plain concept bottleneck, a language model writes the concepts as sentences, and CLIP scores them directly, so nothing is trained to detect concepts. Only the head learns, and it starts from the language prior instead of from scratch.
beats.head: What changed compared with the plain CBM

beats.text: In symbols: g is CLIP itself, so c hat j is 100 times the cosine between the image and sentence j. f is a linear layer that starts from the language prior. The data: images and class labels.
beats.head: LaBo in symbols

beats.text: Label-free models and LaBo share a weakness: nothing checks that a concept is actually visible in the image.
beats.head: Nothing checks that a {c:concept} is really in the {x:image}

beats.text: The fix rests on a simple intuition. Naming a concept is not the same as pointing at it. So ask a detector to point at each concept in the image, and count only the concepts it can find.
beats.head: Naming a {c:concept} is not the same as pointing at it

beats.text: There are three ways a concept can fail. Some are not visual, such as a gull's call. Some describe the setting, not the bird. And some score highly on images that do not contain them, such as a black head on a gull whose head is white.
beats.head: Three ways a {c:concept} can fail

beats.text: Here is why accuracy alone is not enough. Start with a photo and a pretrained image encoder. In this baseline, the concept layer has randomly chosen weights that stay fixed: it was never taught concepts such as yellow bill. Its outputs still depend on the image. Train only the final head using images and their class labels, then test on new images. When the head can use many of these outputs, the paper finds that accuracy can approach that of concept-based models. Useful image information has survived, even though the layer was never trained to detect named concepts. So check whether a high yellow-bill score really corresponds to a yellow bill, as well as checking the predicted class.
beats.head: High accuracy does not prove meaningful {c:concepts}

beats.text: Their method is the Vision-Language-Guided Concept Bottleneck Model, or VLG-CBM. It grounds the concepts first. It uses an open-vocabulary object detector: a detector that can search for any phrase you give it, not only a fixed list of objects. It looks for each concept in each training image, and draws a box where it finds it.
beats.head: VLG-CBM asks a detector to find each {c:concept}

beats.text: A concept counts as present only where a box was found. For our gull, the bill, head and wingtips each get a one, and the call gets a zero. We call this vector c det: the concept labels from the detector.
beats.head: A box means 1, no box means 0

beats.text: These grounded labels train the concept layer: a linear layer that turns the backbone's features into one score per concept. The loss is a binary cross-entropy, as in the original CBM, but no person draws the labels.
beats.head: The {c:grounded labels} train the concept layer with a {l:loss}

beats.text: One term, as in Part 5. The wingtips have a box, so their label is one; if the layer predicts 0.8, the term is minus log 0.8, about 0.22. The call has no box, so its label is zero; a prediction of 0.2 costs the same, minus log of one minus 0.2.
beats.head: One term of the {l:loss}, worked out

beats.text: They also report the number of effective concepts, NEC for short. Each row of the head holds one class's weights, one per concept. Count the non-zero weights in each row, here three, two and four, and average over the classes: the NEC is three.
beats.head: Count the non-zero {f:weights} in each class's row

beats.text: Why does this count matter? A head that puts weight on every concept can fit almost anything. The paper proves that even a random, untrained concept layer can approximate any linear classifier once there are enough concepts. So a dense head can be accurate and still explain nothing.
beats.head: A {f:head} that uses every {c:concept} explains nothing

beats.text: So the fair comparison gives every model the same budget: the same number of concepts per class. Only then does higher accuracy say something about the concepts themselves.
beats.head: A fair comparison: the same number of {c:concepts} per class

beats.text: In symbols, the count for class k is the zero norm of its row of weights: the number of entries that are not zero. The NEC averages that count over the K classes.
beats.head: The same count in symbols

beats.text: The paper reports accuracy with the NEC held at five. A head like that can actually be read: each class rests on a handful of named concepts.
beats.head: Five {c:concepts} per class can actually be read

beats.text: Compared with label-free models, two things change. The concept layer learns from the detector's boxes instead of copying CLIP's scores, and the head is judged at a fixed number of concepts per class.
beats.head: What changed compared with {c:label-free} models

beats.text: In symbols: g is a backbone with a concept layer, W c, trained on the detector labels c det. f is sparse and linear, with the number of effective concepts held fixed. The data: images and class labels, plus a detector.
beats.head: VLG-CBM in symbols

scenes.title: Part 10 · Rung Three: No fitting on the new task

beats.text: On rung three, a pretrained model scores descriptions and a fixed rule combines the scores, without fitting a head to labelled examples from the new task.
beats.head: No fitting on the new task

beats.text: The last step on the ladder removes training altogether. Menon and Vondrick call it classification by description. We shorten this to CBD in our comparison table.
beats.head: The last rung: no training data at all

beats.text: The intuition is a checklist. A language model writes a short checklist for every class. CLIP ticks each item softly, with a score for how well the photo matches it. The class with the best average tick wins.
beats.head: Each {y:class} gets a checklist, and {x:CLIP} ticks it softly

beats.text: A language model writes a few descriptors for every class: short phrases about what the class looks like. For a herring gull: a white body with black wingtips, a yellow beak and legs, a red spot on its beak.
beats.head: A language model describes every {y:class}

beats.text: CLIP scores the image against each descriptor: that score is the soft tick. The class score is simply the average of its descriptors' scores, and the highest average wins.
beats.head: {x:CLIP} scores the photo against each descriptor

beats.text: Where does a score come from? CLIP has two encoders. One, phi, turns the image into a vector; the other, psi, turns the descriptor into a vector in the same space. The score is the cosine similarity of the two: near one when they point the same way, smaller when they do not.
beats.head: One descriptor score: a {c:cosine} between two vectors

beats.text: Then y hat k, the score of class k, averages the descriptor scores over D k, the class's list of descriptors. Nothing is fitted to the target data.
beats.head: The {y:class score} averages its descriptor scores

beats.text: Every prediction comes with its reasons: the descriptor scores that were averaged. On our gull photograph, the five herring gull descriptors score between 0.32 and 0.34, and their average is about 0.33.
beats.head: Every score comes with its reasons

beats.text: But the slaty-backed gull's descriptors average slightly higher, so it edges ahead by a tiny margin. Our photo shows a herring gull, so this prediction is a near miss.
beats.head: Slaty-backed gull edges ahead

beats.text: So when is this attractive? When you have no labelled images at all. And a new class needs only a new description: write its checklist, and it can be scored at once, with no retraining.
beats.head: Attractive when there are no labels at all

beats.text: But the descriptors themselves can be wrong: the language model says a California gull has a black head, which it does not.
beats.head: A descriptor can be wrong

beats.text: Look at our herring gull photo: its head is white and its bill is yellow. The California gull checklist says black head and bill, yet CLIP gives that phrase a positive similarity score. That number compares the photo with the whole phrase; it is not a probability that each detail is true. The fixed average still includes it, so a misleading description can affect the class score. Other descriptions may be impossible to verify from a photo, or describe its background. The takeaway: check that the words are correct and visible, then test whether changing that feature changes its score.
beats.head: A {c:match score} is not a fact check

beats.text: Compared with LaBo, the head is no longer learned. LaBo trained a linear layer on CLIP's sentence scores; here the class score is a fixed average, so nothing is trained and no labelled image is needed.
beats.head: What changed compared with LaBo: the {f:head} is no longer learned

beats.text: In symbols: g is CLIP, c hat d is the similarity to descriptor d, and f is a fixed average over each class's descriptors. The data: none. The cost: nothing guarantees that the descriptors are correct, or grounded.
beats.head: Classification by description in symbols

beats.text: Six variants are a lot to hold in mind at once. This table puts them beside the original CBM, one row per method, and we fill it one column at a time.
beats.head: One table: one row per variant, one column at a time

beats.text: The first column is the data needed for training. Here x is an image, c its concept labels, and y its class label. Supervised CBMs and concept embedding models need all three.
beats.head: Column one: the {y:supervision} each variant needs

beats.text: Post-hoc models, label-free models, LaBo and VLG-CBM drop the concept labels. Classification by description, CBD in the table, needs no training data at all.
beats.head: Most variants drop the {c:concept labels}

beats.text: The second column says who supplies the concepts. For CBMs and concept embedding models, people do, through their labels. The others take them from a concept bank, a language model, CLIP, or a detector.
beats.head: Column two: where the {c:concepts} come from

beats.text: The third column is what the task head actually reads. A CBM passes one number per concept, a concept embedding model a vector per concept, and a post-hoc model its projection scores plus a residual. Label-free models and VLG-CBM pass the outputs of a learned concept layer, and LaBo and classification by description pass raw CLIP scores.
beats.head: Column three: what the {f:task head} reads

beats.text: The last column is what gets trained. CBMs and concept embedding models train the concept predictor and the head. Post-hoc models and LaBo train only the head. Label-free models and VLG-CBM train a concept layer and the head. Classification by description trains nothing at all.
beats.head: Column four: what is trained

beats.text: Each change makes concepts cheaper or predictions more accurate. None makes grounding automatic. A phrase from a language model, or a CLIP similarity, does not show that the model sees that property in the image. That has to be checked.
beats.head: Naming a {c:concept} does not ground it

beats.text: One question sums up the table: who supplies the concepts, and who checks them? In CBMs and concept embedding models, people label the concepts, so people check them. In post-hoc models, a concept bank supplies them, checked only by whoever built it. Label-free models and LaBo take them from a language model, and only a CLIP similarity checks them. VLG-CBM keeps the language model, and adds a detector as the check. In classification by description, nobody checks.
beats.head: Who supplies the {c:concepts}, and who checks them?

beats.text: This is the general trade-off. Each rung up the ladder removes a human labour cost, and with it a human check. The labour saved on labelling has to be spent later, on checking that the concepts are really in the image.
beats.head: Each rung up the ladder removes a cost and a {e:check}

beats.text: How should we judge a concept bottleneck? We need to check the concepts, the predictions and the effect of interventions.
beats.head: Evaluating a concept bottleneck

scenes.title: How should we evaluate a CBM?

beats.text: How should we judge such a model? Accuracy alone hides most of what matters, so we ask four separate questions, each about a different part of the model.
beats.head: Accuracy alone hides most of what a {c:concept bottleneck} promises

beats.text: First, task accuracy: are the predictions correct? In everyday terms, is the final answer right? Measure it on held-out test images, images the model never saw during training.
beats.head: Task accuracy: are the {y:predictions} correct?

beats.text: The formula only counts. The bracket is 1 when the prediction matches the true label, and 0 when it does not. Add up the ones and divide by the number of images. Three predictions with two right give an accuracy of two thirds.
beats.head: Task accuracy counts the right {y:answers}

beats.text: Second, concept accuracy: are the concept estimates correct? In everyday terms, did the model read the evidence correctly? Take one test image, a small red square. Round each concept score to 0 or 1, and compare it with the label. Large scores 0.78, which rounds to 1, but the square is small, so its label is 0. Four of the five match. Concept accuracy averages these matches over all images and all concepts.
beats.head: Concept accuracy: are the {c:concept values} right?

beats.text: The second question has a second half, grounding: does each estimate rest on the intended evidence? A score for wingtip black should come from the wingtip, not from the water. So we also check where the detector looks.
beats.head: Grounding: does each {c:concept} rest on the right evidence?

beats.text: Third, faithfulness: does the output actually depend on the concepts, in the way the model claims? An explanation is faithful when it tells the truth about how the answer was made. To test it, change a concept and check that the output moves as the head says. In the gull head from Part 2, setting wingtip black to 1 lifts herring gull from 0.29 to 0.91.
beats.head: Faithfulness: does the {y:output} really depend on the {c:concepts}?

beats.text: Fourth, intervention utility: when a person corrects a concept, do decisions improve, and at what human cost? Correct concepts one at a time, and plot accuracy against the number of corrections. Each correction costs a person's time, so a curve that rises early is better.
beats.head: Intervention utility: do {e:corrections} help, and at what cost?

beats.text: Here is a real experiment where we know every true concept. The images are synthetic, 64 by 64 pixels: each shape is red or blue, a circle or a square, small or large. Two colours, two shapes and two sizes give eight classes. Five yes-or-no concepts describe each image: red, blue, circle, square and large. Together they fully determine the class.
beats.head: A controlled test: synthetic shapes with known {c:concepts}

beats.text: Three models share the same small CNN, the same data, and the same training budget of 60 epochs, that is, 60 passes through the 768 training images. The black box predicts the class directly. The multi-task model also predicts the concepts, with a concept head beside its class head. The strict CBM predicts the concepts first, and its head reads only those five values.
beats.head: Three models share one small {x:CNN}

beats.text: Each bar is the share of the 512 test images classified correctly: 78.7 percent for the black box, 82.0 for multi-task, and 81.6 for the strict CBM. On this question alone, the three look about the same.
beats.head: Task accuracy: the three models are close

beats.text: Over all images and all five concepts, the strict CBM gets 92.4 percent of its concept values right. The bars on the left split this by concept. Colour is always right, and shape is hardest, at about 84 percent for circle and 83 for square.
beats.head: Concept accuracy: most {c:concept values} are right

beats.text: Back to our test image, the small red square. Its concept large reads 0.78, so the model believes the square is large, and the head predicts large red square. A person sets large to 0, and the same head now predicts small red square, the true class.
beats.head: One {e:edit} to one {c:concept} changes the {y:prediction}

beats.text: Now do this for every test image. The true labels play a perfect expert, which we call an oracle. It fixes the concept with the largest error first. For our square, that is large, which is 0.78 away from its label of 0.
beats.head: {e:Oracle corrections}: fix the worst {c:concept} first

beats.text: On this chart, the horizontal axis counts corrections per image, from 0 to 5, and the vertical axis shows task accuracy, starting at 80 percent. One oracle correction lifts accuracy from 81.6 to 97.3 percent. With all five corrected, it reaches 100.
beats.head: Each step right is one more {e:correction} per image

beats.text: Now pick the concept to correct at random instead. The dashed line rises more slowly: 87.3 percent after one correction, averaged over 32 random orders. A random pick often fixes a concept that was already right, as four of the five were for our square. The shaded band spans the lowest and highest of the 32 runs.
beats.head: {e:Random corrections} help more slowly

beats.text: Now the multi-task model. Edit its concept head, and its class scores stay exactly the same, because its class head never reads the concepts.
beats.head: In the multi-task model, a {e:concept edit} changes nothing

beats.text: Read these numbers with care: one training seed, meaning a single training run, 512 synthetic test images, and corrections taken from the true labels, standing in for a perfect, effortless expert. Real experts make mistakes, and their time is costly.
beats.head: Read these numbers with care

beats.text: The three models have similar accuracy, yet they differ completely in intervention utility. Each metric measures a different property.
beats.head: Similar accuracy, very different intervention utility

beats.text: Why can similar accuracy hide such different behaviour? Accuracy marks only the final answer, not the route to it. The multi-task model's class head never reads its concept estimates, so fixing one is like correcting a note that nobody reads. In the strict CBM, the concepts are the only road to the answer, so a fix reaches the prediction.
beats.head: Why similar accuracy can hide very different {e:intervention utility}

beats.text: The bottleneck idea also applies to other kinds of input, provided the intermediate concepts have a useful meaning.
beats.head: Beyond images

beats.text: So far our inputs were photographs of birds. Concept bottlenecks fit wherever experts already reason with named findings, the things they check and write down by name.
beats.head: Where else do {c:concept bottlenecks} fit?

beats.text: In medicine, Koh and colleagues also trained a CBM on knee X-rays from the Osteoarthritis Initiative. The model first scores ten clinical findings, such as joint space narrowing and bone spurs, each on a small scale of its own. From those, the head predicts how severe the osteoarthritis is, on four levels from 0 to 3.
beats.head: Medicine: a knee {x:X-ray} → clinical {c:findings} → a severity {y:grade}

beats.text: A radiologist can correct a finding, and the grade is recomputed. Here, joint space narrowing goes from 1 to 2, and the grade goes from 2 to 3. Radiologists already write their reports in these terms.
beats.head: A radiologist {e:corrects} a finding, and the {y:grade} is recomputed

beats.text: In language, the CEBaB benchmark annotates restaurant reviews with four concepts: food, service, ambiance and noise. In this review the food is praised and the service is criticised, while ambiance and noise are not mentioned. Text bottleneck models predict the star rating from those concept values, so you can see which aspect drove it. Reviewers already write this way.
beats.head: Language: a {x:review} → four {c:aspects} → a star {y:rating}

beats.text: In intensive care, Wu and colleagues built concept bottlenecks on patients' time series, measurements recorded over time. The task is vasopressor onset: when a patient will need vasopressors, drugs that support blood pressure. The concepts are summaries learned without concept labels, close to how doctors already sum up a patient, in terms like illness severity and kidney function.
beats.head: Intensive care: {x:vital signs} → summary {c:concepts} → {y:drugs needed soon?}

beats.text: In wearable sensing, X-CHAR explains a complex activity through the simpler activities it is made of, which a person can recognise in the sensor signal. In its nurse data, the simple activities include check vitals, collect blood and oral care. People already describe a complex activity as the simple steps it is made of.
beats.head: Wearables: {x:sensor signal} → simple {c:activities} → complex {y:activity}

beats.text: And in sleep staging, the concepts are the patterns that scorers already use, as in Part 6: spindles, K-complexes and slow waves. The head turns them into a sleep stage, such as stage two. Scorers already mark these patterns by hand, so each concept matches a mark they would make.
beats.head: Sleep: an {x:EEG} → the {c:patterns} scorers use → a sleep {y:stage}

beats.text: The recipe is the same each time. Name the findings an expert checks, predict them from the raw signal, and let the decision depend on them alone.
beats.head: One recipe in every domain

scenes.title: Part 13: What can still go wrong?

beats.text: An editable concept interface is useful, but we still need to check how it behaves and what its scores mean.
beats.head: What can still go wrong?

scenes.title: An interpretable interface is not the end of the story

beats.text: Readable concepts in the middle do not guarantee a good model. Let us follow the path from the photo x, through the concept scores c hat, to the answer y hat, and ask what can fail at each of five points.
beats.head: Follow the path from {x:photo} to {c:concepts} to {y:answer}: what can fail?

beats.text: First, distribution shift: the encoder meets data unlike its training data. In symbols, new inputs come from a different distribution than the training inputs. Recall the chest X-ray model from Part 1.
beats.head: 1 · {x:Encoder}: distribution shift

beats.text: Its AUC, a score where 1 means perfect ranking and 0.5 means guessing, was about 0.93 on X-rays from the hospitals it learned from, and about 0.82 at a new hospital. In practice, the model looks fine where it was built and does worse at the new site.
beats.head: A new hospital: the same model scores lower

beats.text: Second, wrong grounding: the concept detector responds to the wrong evidence, such as the water behind a gull instead of its wingtip. In practice, the score looks right for the wrong reason, until a gull turns up away from water.
beats.head: 2 · {x:Concept detector}: wrong grounding

beats.text: Third, missing information: the vocabulary leaves out what the task needs. In Part 8, a blue circle and a blue square shared one concept vector, so the best any head could do was guess, right half the time. In practice, two cases an expert would tell apart look identical to the head.
beats.head: 3 · {c:Vocabulary}: missing information

beats.text: Fourth, the task head can learn the wrong relationship. Recall the billing head from Part 7: it takes away 2 for each unit of duplicate charge, the wrong sign. A correct edit sets duplicate charge to 1, and billing falls from 0.80 to 0.45. In practice, the expert's fix is right, yet the decision moves the wrong way.
beats.head: 4 · {f:Task head}: the wrong relationship

beats.text: Fifth, the intervention can be wrong, or too costly. On this chart from Part 11, each step to the right is one more correction per image, and each correction takes an expert's time. Ours came from true labels, an expert who never errs. In practice, a busy expert can misjudge a concept too, and every check uses time they could spend elsewhere.
beats.head: 5 · {e:Intervention}: wrong, or too costly

beats.text: So ask five questions of any concept bottleneck. Are the concepts meaningful? Are they grounded correctly? Are they sufficient for the task? Does the model actually use them? And do corrections improve decisions?
beats.head: Five questions for any {c:concept bottleneck}

beats.text: Knab and colleagues' 2026 survey organises the field around the same parts: the input, the concepts, the output and the training. It lists these issues among its open challenges.
beats.head: A 2026 survey maps the field onto the same parts

beats.text: We finish by following the whole path again, from an image through concepts to a prediction and an intervention.
beats.head: Putting the pieces together

beats.text: One last time, the gull. A black box maps the photograph straight to a species.
beats.head: One last time: a black box maps the {x:photo} to a {y:species}

beats.text: Open it up. Input. Encoder. Concept predictor. Named concepts. Task head. Prediction.
beats.head: Open it: {c:named concepts} sit on the path to the {y:prediction}

beats.text: A person sees that the wingtips are black and corrects that concept. The head now says American herring gull, at 0.91.
beats.head: A person {e:corrects} one concept, and the {y:prediction} follows

beats.text: But the interface is only as good as its parts: the concepts it names, where they look, and the head that reads them. A concept may be missing, a detector may look at the water, and a head may hold a wrong rule.
beats.head: The interface is only as good as its parts

beats.text: In short, concept bottleneck models put named values that people can read in the middle of a prediction. Those values can be inspected, evaluated, and sometimes corrected.
beats.head: {c:Concepts} that can be inspected, evaluated and {e:corrected}

beats.text: The challenge is to make sure the interface faithfully represents the information on which the prediction depends. Put simply, whatever the answer uses should be visible in the concepts.
beats.head: The interface must carry what the {y:prediction} depends on

beats.text: Four things to remember. Post-hoc methods explain a model after the fact, while a concept bottleneck makes the answer pass through named concepts. Fixing a concept helps only if the head reads it the right way. A soft score can carry more than its name says, and that extra information leaks to the head. And newer variants find concepts with fewer labels, so check that each one looks at the right evidence.
beats.head: What to remember

scenes.title: Appendix: Testing concept use in a black box

beats.text: The appendix introduces testing with concept activation vectors, a way to ask whether a black-box model responds to a named concept.
beats.head: Testing concept use in a black box

scenes.title: Appendix: testing with concept activation vectors

beats.text: This appendix adds one more post-hoc method, one that asks about concepts directly. Testing with concept activation vectors, or TCAV, asks a question like this one: does the model use grey wings when it says herring gull? Here the model is CLIP, the black box from Part 1.
beats.head: TCAV asks about a named {c:concept}: does the model use {c:grey wings} when it says {y:herring gull}?

beats.text: The first step is to collect example photos: some birds with grey wings, and some without, here from a labelled bird dataset. None of them is a herring gull.
beats.head: Step 1: collect photos {c:with grey wings} and photos {m:without}

beats.text: Pass every photo through the model and look at its internal activations. Fit a line that separates the two groups. The direction across that line is the concept activation vector: moving along it means more grey wing.
beats.head: Step 2: the {c:concept direction} separates them inside the model

beats.text: Now take a herring gull photo and ask: if its activation moved a little in the grey wing direction, would the herring gull score go up? The gradient of the score, times the direction, gives the answer as a sign.
beats.head: Step 3: nudge each {y:herring gull} photo along that direction

beats.text: The TCAV score is the share of herring gull photos where the score goes up. For grey wings, it went up for almost all 60 photos, in each of 10 repeats with different example photos.
beats.head: The TCAV score: the share of photos whose {y:score} rises

beats.text: A direction that separates two random sets of photos gives scores that jump between zero and one. So a concept counts only when its score is steady and different from random ones. And even then, TCAV says what the model responds to. It gives no way to correct it.
beats.head: Compare with random directions

beats.text: Concept Bottleneck Models. Predicting through interpretable concepts.
